mock_title: CLAT PG (LL.M.) Full-Length Mock Test - 02 (Constitutional Amendments Special)

pattern.note: The official CLAT PG paper has 120 MCQs/120 marks/120 minutes, built on passage-based questions. This mock is extended to 150 questions, as in Mock 01; scale to 120 by dropping any 5 passages if you want exact parity. Fourteen of the 25 passages (84 questions) are Constitutional Law, centred on the most repeatable constitutional amendments and the cases that interpret them.

instructions: Each question carries 1 mark; 0.25 marks deducted for each wrong answer.
Answer from the passage and the legal principles stated or implied; read every option.

Passages summarise the law and leading cases as understood at the time of preparation; where a passage flags a matter as pending or evolving (for example the 2023 Election Commissioners Act), verify its current status before citing it in exam answers.

passages.title: Article 368, Golak Nath and the Basic Structure Doctrine
passages.passage: Article 368 deals with the power of Parliament to amend the Constitution. In Shankari Prasad (1951) and Sajjan Singh (1965), the Supreme Court held that the word 'law' in Article 13(2) did not include constitutional amendments, so that Fundamental Rights could be amended. In I.C. Golak Nath v. State of Punjab (1967), an eleven-judge Bench reversed this by a majority of 6:5, holding that an amendment is 'law' under Article 13(2) and that Parliament could not abridge Fundamental Rights. Parliament responded with the Constitution (Twenty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1971, which added clause (4) to Article 13 to exclude constitutional amendments from its scope, and amended Article 368 to confer the 'power' to amend expressly and to make presidential assent to an amendment Bill obligatory. In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), a thirteen-judge Bench, by a majority of 7:6, overruled Golak Nath and upheld the 24th Amendment, but held that the amending power does not extend to altering the 'basic structure' of the Constitution. In Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975), the Court struck down clause (4) of Article 329A, inserted by the 39th Amendment, which sought to validate the Prime Minister's election set aside by the Allahabad High Court, since it exercised judicial power through legislation and offended free and fair elections and the rule of law. The Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976 then inserted clauses (4) and (5) in Article 368, providing that no amendment could be questioned in any court and that the amending power had no limits. In Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980), the Court struck down both clauses, reasoning that a limited amending power is itself a basic feature and that Parliament cannot, by exercising a limited power, enlarge it into an absolute one.

questions.question: The decision which held that an amendment under Article 368 is 'law' within Article 13(2), so that Parliament could not abridge Fundamental Rights, is

options.A: Sajjan Singh v. State of Rajasthan
options.B: Shankari Prasad v. Union of India
options.C: I.C. Golak Nath v. State of Punjab
options.D: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala

questions.explanation: The passage attributes this holding to Golak Nath (1967, 6:5). Shankari Prasad and Sajjan Singh held the opposite, and Kesavananda overruled Golak Nath.

questions.question: The Twenty-fourth Amendment, 1971 did which of the following?

options.A: Added Article 13(4) and made assent to amendment Bills obligatory
options.B: Inserted clauses (4) and (5) in Article 368 to bar judicial review of amendments
options.C: Validated the Prime Minister's election by inserting Article 329A(4)
options.D: Declared that the basic structure of the Constitution cannot be amended

questions.explanation: The 24th Amendment added Article 13(4) and amended Article 368 for the power to amend and compulsory assent. Clauses 368(4)-(5) came with the 42nd Amendment; Article 329A(4) with the 39th; the basic structure doctrine is judicial, from Kesavananda.

questions.question: Which of the following gives the correct chronological order of events described in the passage?

options.A: Golak Nath, 24th Amendment, Kesavananda, Raj Narain, 42nd Amendment, Minerva Mills
options.B: Golak Nath, Kesavananda, 24th Amendment, 42nd Amendment, Raj Narain, Minerva Mills
options.C: Kesavananda, Golak Nath, 24th Amendment, Raj Narain, Minerva Mills, 42nd Amendment
options.D: 24th Amendment, Golak Nath, Kesavananda, 42nd Amendment, Raj Narain, Minerva Mills

questions.explanation: Golak Nath (1967), 24th Amendment (1971), Kesavananda (1973), Raj Narain (1975), 42nd Amendment (1976), Minerva Mills (1980).

questions.question: In Minerva Mills, clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368 were struck down because

options.A: Parliament has no power whatever to amend Article 368, which is itself part of the basic structure
options.B: the clauses were not passed by two-thirds of the members present and voting in each House
options.C: the clauses had not been ratified by the legislatures of half of the States as the proviso requires
options.D: a limited amending power is itself basic, so Parliament cannot make it absolute

questions.explanation: The passage states the Court's reasoning: a limited amending power is a basic feature and cannot be enlarged into an absolute one. The other reasons are not given.

questions.question: Parliament passes a constitutional amendment declaring that the election of a named Member of Parliament, set aside by a High Court for corrupt practice, 'shall be valid and shall not be called in question in any court'. On the principles in the passage, the amendment is most likely to be

options.A: upheld, because Article 368 permits amendments to be placed beyond judicial review altogether
options.B: upheld, because it was passed by the requisite special majority under Article 368(2)
options.C: treated as a non-justiciable political question that courts cannot decide
options.D: struck down, as it usurps judicial power and offends free and fair elections

questions.explanation: This mirrors Article 329A(4), struck down in Raj Narain for the reasons stated in the passage. A special majority cannot save an amendment that violates the basic structure.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT consistent with the holding in Kesavananda Bharati as described in the passage?

options.A: Parliament cannot amend any Fundamental Right in any manner whatsoever
options.B: An amendment that alters the basic structure is open to invalidation by courts
options.C: Golak Nath no longer represents the law on the amending power
options.D: The Twenty-fourth Amendment was constitutionally valid

questions.explanation: Kesavananda overruled Golak Nath's total bar on amending Fundamental Rights; rights may be amended so long as the basic structure is not altered.

passages.title: Emergency Provisions: The 44th Amendment, ADM Jabalpur and S.R. Bommai
passages.passage: The Constitution provides for national emergency (Article 352), failure of constitutional machinery in a State (Article 356) and financial emergency (Article 360). Article 352 originally permitted a proclamation on the ground of 'internal disturbance', the ground invoked in 1975. The Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978 substituted 'armed rebellion' and provided that the President may proclaim an emergency only on the written decision of the Union Cabinet. A proclamation must be approved by each House by a special majority within one month and, once approved, ceases to operate after six months from the date of the second approving resolution unless re-approved. A resolution disapproving the proclamation may be passed by a simple majority of the Lok Sabha, which must meet within fourteen days if one-tenth of its members give notice. Article 358 automatically suspends the freedoms under Article 19 when an emergency is declared on the ground of war or external aggression, but not on the ground of armed rebellion. Under Article 359, the President may by order suspend the right to move courts for enforcing Fundamental Rights, but, after the 44th Amendment, not the rights under Articles 20 and 21. In ADM Jabalpur v. Shivakant Shukla (1976), a majority held that during the Emergency no person could move a court to challenge detention under Article 21; Justice H.R. Khanna dissented. That decision was overruled in K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017). In S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), a nine-judge Bench held that a proclamation under Article 356 is subject to judicial review, that the Assembly should not be dissolved before Parliament approves the proclamation, that a floor test is the proper method of testing a Chief Minister's majority, and that secularism is a basic feature of the Constitution.

questions.question: The expression substituted for 'internal disturbance' in Article 352 by the 44th Amendment is

options.A: external aggression
options.B: breakdown of public order
options.C: armed rebellion
options.D: failure of constitutional machinery

questions.explanation: The passage states that the 44th Amendment substituted 'armed rebellion' for 'internal disturbance'.

questions.question: Which Fundamental Rights cannot be suspended by a Presidential order under Article 359 after the 44th Amendment?

options.A: The rights under Articles 19 and 21
options.B: The rights under Articles 25 and 26
options.C: The rights under Articles 20 and 21
options.D: The rights under Articles 14 and 15

questions.explanation: After the 44th Amendment, the enforcement of Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended under Article 359. Article 19 can be suspended.

questions.question: An emergency is proclaimed on the ground of external aggression. Which consequence follows automatically under the passage, without any further Presidential order?

options.A: The rights under Articles 20 and 21 stand suspended
options.B: The Lok Sabha stands dissolved
options.C: The right to move the Supreme Court under Article 32 is abolished
options.D: The freedoms under Article 19 stand suspended

questions.explanation: Article 358 automatically suspends Article 19 on a war or external aggression emergency. Articles 20 and 21 can never be suspended, and the other consequences are not provided.

questions.question: An emergency is proclaimed on the ground of armed rebellion, and the President by order suspends the enforcement of Articles 19, 20 and 21. On the passage, the order is

options.A: effective only as to Article 19, since Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended
options.B: wholly valid, since Article 359 permits suspension of every Fundamental Right
options.C: wholly invalid, since Article 19 stands automatically suspended under Article 358 and needs no order
options.D: wholly invalid, since an emergency cannot be proclaimed on the ground of armed rebellion

questions.explanation: Article 358 does not operate for armed rebellion, so an Article 359 order is needed for Article 19; but Articles 20 and 21 are protected from suspension. Armed rebellion is a valid ground after the 44th Amendment.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a proposition laid down in S.R. Bommai as described in the passage?

options.A: The Governor's report is conclusive and cannot be examined by any court
options.B: A proclamation under Article 356 is subject to judicial review by the courts
options.C: A floor test is the proper way to test a Chief Minister's majority in the House
options.D: Secularism is a basic feature of the Constitution of India

questions.explanation: Bommai made proclamations judicially reviewable; it did not treat the Governor's report as conclusive.

questions.question: A proclamation of national emergency is approved by the second House on 25 January. Under the passage, unless re-approved, it ceases to operate on

options.A: 25 February of the same year
options.B: 25 April of the same year
options.C: 25 July of the same year
options.D: 25 January of the following year

questions.explanation: A proclamation ceases six months after the date of the second approving resolution: 25 July.

passages.title: Right to Property: From Article 31 to Article 300A, and the Ninth Schedule
passages.passage: The framers guaranteed the right to property in Articles 19(1)(f) and 31. When courts insisted on compensation, Parliament amended the Constitution repeatedly. In State of West Bengal v. Bela Banerjee (1954), the Supreme Court held that compensation under Article 31(2) must be a just equivalent of what the owner was deprived of. The Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951 had already inserted Article 31A, saving laws for the acquisition of estates, and Article 31B, which validates laws placed in the Ninth Schedule notwithstanding any judicial decision. The Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, 1955 provided that the adequacy of compensation could not be questioned in court, and the Seventeenth Amendment (1964) enlarged the definition of 'estate' and added many land reform laws to the Ninth Schedule. The Twenty-fifth Amendment (1971) replaced 'compensation' in Article 31(2) with 'amount' and inserted Article 31C. The Forty-fourth Amendment (1978) deleted Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31 and inserted Article 300A, which provides that no person shall be deprived of property save by authority of law. Property thus ceased to be a Fundamental Right and became a constitutional right. In Waman Rao v. Union of India (1981), the Court held that Articles 31A and 31B remain valid for laws placed in the Ninth Schedule before 24 April 1973, the date of Kesavananda Bharati. In I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007), a nine-judge Bench held that a law placed in the Ninth Schedule after that date is open to challenge if it violates Fundamental Rights forming part of the basic structure. In Vidya Devi v. State of Himachal Pradesh (2020), the Court held that, although no longer fundamental, the right to property remains a human right and a constitutional right under Article 300A, and the State cannot take property by executive action without the authority of law.

questions.question: Article 31B and the Ninth Schedule were inserted by the

options.A: First Amendment, 1951
options.B: Fourth Amendment, 1955
options.C: Forty-fourth Amendment, 1978
options.D: Twenty-fifth Amendment, 1971

questions.explanation: The passage states that the First Amendment inserted Articles 31A and 31B (with the Ninth Schedule).

questions.question: After the Forty-fourth Amendment, the right to property is

options.A: no longer protected by any provision of the Constitution
options.B: a constitutional right under Article 300A, but not a Fundamental Right
options.C: a Directive Principle of State Policy
options.D: a Fundamental Right under Article 19(1)(f)

questions.explanation: The 44th Amendment deleted Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 and inserted Article 300A, making it a constitutional right.

questions.question: Which amendment sought to overcome the view in Bela Banerjee by providing that the adequacy of compensation could not be questioned in court?

options.A: The Fourth Amendment, 1955
options.B: The First Amendment, 1951
options.C: The Twenty-fifth Amendment, 1971
options.D: The Seventeenth Amendment, 1964

questions.explanation: Bela Banerjee required a just equivalent; the Fourth Amendment made adequacy non-justiciable.

questions.question: A land reform law is placed in the Ninth Schedule in 2005 and is challenged as violating Articles 14 and 21. Under the passage, the Court

options.A: must uphold it, since Article 31B validates laws in the Ninth Schedule notwithstanding any judicial decision
options.B: may not examine it, since property is no longer a Fundamental Right
options.C: may examine whether the violation damages or destroys the basic structure, and strike the law down if it does
options.D: may examine it only if the law was placed in the Ninth Schedule before 24 April 1973

questions.explanation: I.R. Coelho held that Ninth Schedule laws placed after 24 April 1973 are open to challenge on basic structure grounds.

questions.question: A State takes possession of a farmer's land by an executive order, without any statute authorising acquisition, on the footing that property is no longer a Fundamental Right. On the passage, the action is

options.A: unconstitutional, since Article 300A requires authority of law
options.B: valid on payment of an 'amount' under Article 31(2)
options.C: valid, since Vidya Devi permits executive deprivation in the public interest
options.D: valid, since the right to property is no longer enforceable in any court

questions.explanation: Vidya Devi held that the State cannot take property by executive action without the authority of law. Article 31 was deleted by the 44th Amendment.

questions.question: A law placed in the Ninth Schedule on 1 January 1970 is challenged in 2010 as violating Article 14. On Waman Rao and Coelho as described, the law

options.A: is open to challenge, since every Ninth Schedule law is reviewable on the basic structure test
options.B: remains protected, since it was placed in the Ninth Schedule before 24 April 1973
options.C: is protected only if compensation was paid to the owners
options.D: is void, since the Ninth Schedule itself is unconstitutional

questions.explanation: Waman Rao preserved the protection of Articles 31A and 31B for laws placed before 24 April 1973; Coelho's review applies to laws placed after that date.

passages.title: The 73rd and 74th Amendments: Panchayats and Municipalities
passages.passage: The Constitution (Seventy-third Amendment) Act, 1992 inserted Part IX (Articles 243 to 243O) and the Eleventh Schedule, listing twenty-nine subjects, and came into force on 24 April 1993. The Seventy-fourth Amendment, in force from 1 June 1993, inserted Part IXA (Articles 243P to 243ZG) and the Twelfth Schedule, listing eighteen subjects. Article 243A recognises the Gram Sabha, and Article 243B requires a three-tier Panchayat system, though States with a population not exceeding twenty lakh need not constitute Panchayats at the intermediate level. Seats are filled by direct election; seats are reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in proportion to their population, and not less than one-third of the total seats, including seats reserved for women of those categories, are reserved for women. Offices of chairpersons are reserved on a similar pattern. Under Article 243E, every Panchayat continues for five years, and if it is dissolved earlier, an election must be completed within six months, the new body serving only for the remainder of the unexpired term. A State Finance Commission is constituted every five years under Article 243I, and Article 243K vests the superintendence of Panchayat elections in a State Election Commission. Article 243M excludes Fifth and Sixth Schedule areas from Part IX, subject to Parliament extending it, which it did through the PESA Act, 1996. In Vikas Kishanrao Gawali v. State of Maharashtra (2021), the Supreme Court held that reservation for Other Backward Classes in local bodies requires a 'triple test': a dedicated Commission must conduct an empirical inquiry into backwardness; the proportion of reservation for each local body must be specified in the light of the Commission's recommendations; and the total reservation for SC, ST and OBC must not exceed fifty per cent.

questions.question: The functions of Municipalities are listed in the

options.A: Tenth Schedule
options.B: Ninth Schedule
options.C: Twelfth Schedule
options.D: Eleventh Schedule

questions.explanation: The 74th Amendment inserted Part IXA and the Twelfth Schedule (18 subjects). The Eleventh Schedule concerns Panchayats.

questions.question: Superintendence of the conduct of Panchayat elections vests in the

options.A: Gram Sabha
options.B: Election Commission of India
options.C: State Finance Commission
options.D: State Election Commission

questions.explanation: Article 243K vests superintendence of Panchayat elections in a State Election Commission.

questions.question: A Panchayat constituted for five years is dissolved by the State after two years. Under Article 243E as described,

options.A: an election must be held within one year, and the new body serves a full five-year term
options.B: the State may govern through an administrator until the original five-year term ends
options.C: an election must be held within three months, and the new body serves for two years
options.D: an election must be completed within six months, and the new body serves only the remaining three years

questions.explanation: A new body elected after premature dissolution serves only the unexpired remainder of the term (three years here), and the election must be completed within six months.

questions.question: A State has a population of eighteen lakh. Under Article 243B as described, the State

options.A: need not constitute the intermediate tier, but must have the other tiers
options.B: need not constitute any Panchayats at the village level either
options.C: must constitute all three tiers regardless of its population
options.D: may constitute an intermediate tier only with Presidential approval

questions.explanation: States with population not exceeding twenty lakh may dispense with the intermediate tier only.

questions.question: A Panchayat has 60 seats filled by direct election. The minimum number of seats that must be reserved for women, including women belonging to SC and ST, is
questions.explanation: Not less than one-third of total seats (60/3 = 20), including SC/ST women's seats, must be reserved for women.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an element of the 'triple test' for OBC reservation in local bodies as described?

options.A: Keeping total reservation for SC, ST and OBC within fifty per cent
options.B: Prior approval of Parliament for the reservation in each local body
options.C: An empirical inquiry into backwardness by a dedicated Commission
options.D: Specifying the proportion of reservation for each local body in the light of the Commission's recommendations

questions.explanation: The three elements are the dedicated Commission's empirical inquiry, local-body-wise proportions, and the fifty per cent cap. Parliamentary approval is not part of the test.

passages.title: The 101st Amendment: GST, Article 246A and the GST Council
passages.passage: The Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016 introduced the Goods and Services Tax (GST). Article 246A gives Parliament and State Legislatures concurrent power to make laws on GST, but Parliament has exclusive power over GST on supplies in the course of inter-State trade or commerce. Under Article 269A, GST on inter-State supplies is levied and collected by the Government of India and apportioned between the Union and the States. Article 366(12A) defines GST as any tax on the supply of goods or services or both, except taxes on the supply of alcoholic liquor for human consumption. Crude petroleum, high speed diesel, motor spirit, natural gas and aviation turbine fuel fall within the definition but were kept out of the levy until the Council recommends a date. Article 279A creates the GST Council, chaired by the Union Finance Minister, with Union and State Ministers as members. A quorum is one-half of the members. Every decision requires a majority of not less than three-fourths of the weighted votes of members present and voting, the Union's vote carrying a weightage of one-third and the votes of all States taken together two-thirds. The Council makes recommendations on matters such as tax rates, exemptions and model laws. In Mohit Minerals Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India (2022), the Supreme Court held that the Council's recommendations are not binding on the Union or the States. Because Article 246A confers simultaneous powers on Parliament and State Legislatures, and Article 279A speaks only of 'recommendations', the Court treated them as the product of a collaborative dialogue, having persuasive value and reflecting cooperative federalism.

questions.question: Which of the following is excluded from the definition of GST in Article 366(12A)?

options.A: Tax on the supply of alcoholic liquor for human consumption
options.B: Tax on the supply of services of every kind
options.C: Tax on the supply of crude petroleum and other petroleum products
options.D: Tax on the supply of natural gas and aviation turbine fuel

questions.explanation: Only alcoholic liquor for human consumption is excluded from the definition. Petroleum products fall within it but the levy was deferred until the Council recommends a date.

questions.question: The GST Council is established by

options.A: Article 366(12A)
options.B: Article 246A
options.C: Article 269A
options.D: Article 279A

questions.explanation: Article 279A creates the Council; Article 246A gives legislative power; Article 269A deals with inter-State levy; Article 366(12A) defines GST.

questions.question: Which statement about voting in the GST Council, as described, is correct?

options.A: The Union can pass a decision on its own with its one-third weightage
options.B: Decisions require only a simple majority of the weighted votes
options.C: The Union can block any decision on its own, and the States together cannot pass a decision without the Union's support
options.D: The States together can pass any decision without the Union, since they hold two-thirds of the weighted votes

questions.explanation: A decision needs three-fourths. The Union's one-third exceeds the one-fourth needed to block, while the States' two-thirds is below three-fourths.

questions.question: A State Legislature enacts a GST law that departs from a Council recommendation on the tax rate. Under Mohit Minerals as described, the State law is

options.A: valid only if the Council later ratifies it by a three-fourths majority of weighted votes
options.B: invalid, since Article 279A makes the Council's recommendations binding on all States
options.C: valid only if the Union Government consents to the departure from the Council's rate
options.D: not invalid merely for departing, since recommendations are persuasive, not binding

questions.explanation: Mohit Minerals held that the recommendations are not binding on the Union or the States.

questions.question: A dealer in Chhattisgarh supplies goods to a buyer in Maharashtra. The power to make a law imposing GST on this inter-State supply belongs to

options.A: Parliament exclusively, the tax being levied and collected by the Union
options.B: the Chhattisgarh Legislature exclusively, being the State of origin
options.C: the Maharashtra Legislature exclusively, being the State of destination
options.D: Parliament and both State Legislatures concurrently, in equal measure

questions.explanation: Articles 246A and 269A give Parliament exclusive power over inter-State supplies, levied and collected by the Union.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a reason given in Mohit Minerals for treating Council recommendations as non-binding?

options.A: Article 279A speaks only of 'recommendations'
options.B: The recommendations reflect a collaborative dialogue and cooperative federalism
options.C: Article 246A confers simultaneous legislative powers on Parliament and State Legislatures
options.D: Article 279A requires State Legislatures to adopt the recommendations without modification

questions.explanation: The reasoning rests on simultaneous powers under Article 246A, the wording of Article 279A, and cooperative federalism. A duty to adopt recommendations verbatim is contrary to the holding.

passages.title: Reservation Amendments: 77th, 81st, 82nd, 85th, 102nd, 103rd and 105th
passages.passage: Article 16(4) permits reservation in appointments for backward classes not adequately represented in State services. In Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992), a nine-judge Bench upheld twenty-seven per cent reservation for Other Backward Classes, excluded the 'creamy layer', fixed fifty per cent as the general ceiling save in extraordinary situations, and held that Article 16(4) does not permit reservation in promotions. Parliament responded through a series of amendments. The Seventy-seventh Amendment (1995) inserted Article 16(4A), enabling reservation in promotion for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes inadequately represented in services. The Eighty-first Amendment (2000) inserted Article 16(4B), under which unfilled reserved vacancies carried forward are treated as a separate class and are not counted with the vacancies of the year for the fifty per cent ceiling. The Eighty-second Amendment added a proviso to Article 335 permitting relaxation in qualifying marks in promotion, and the Eighty-fifth Amendment gave consequential seniority. In M. Nagaraj v. Union of India (2006), these amendments were upheld, but the State must collect quantifiable data on backwardness and inadequacy of representation and must preserve administrative efficiency. The Constitution (One Hundred and Third Amendment) Act, 2019 inserted Articles 15(6) and 16(6), allowing up to ten per cent reservation for economically weaker sections other than classes covered by Articles 15(4), 15(5) and 16(4). In Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India (2022), a Constitution Bench upheld it by 3:2, holding that economic criteria do not violate the basic structure and that the fifty per cent ceiling applies to reservations for SC, ST and OBC and not to this new category. The One Hundred and Second Amendment created the National Commission for Backward Classes (Article 338B) and inserted Article 342A; in Jayashree Patil (2021), a majority read it as taking away the States' power to identify socially and educationally backward classes, and the One Hundred and Fifth Amendment (2021) restored the power of States to prepare their own lists.

questions.question: Reservation in promotion for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes was enabled by the insertion of

options.A: Article 16(4B) by the Seventy-seventh Amendment
options.B: Article 16(4A) by the Seventy-seventh Amendment
options.C: Article 342A by the One Hundred and Second Amendment
options.D: Article 15(6) by the Eighty-first Amendment

questions.explanation: The 77th Amendment inserted Article 16(4A); 16(4B) (carry forward) came with the 81st.

questions.question: The Supreme Court decided the challenge to the EWS reservation in Janhit Abhiyan by

options.A: striking down the Amendment unanimously
options.B: upholding the Amendment unanimously
options.C: upholding the Amendment by a 3:2 majority
options.D: striking down the Amendment by a 3:2 majority

questions.explanation: The passage records that the Constitution Bench upheld the 103rd Amendment by 3:2.

questions.question: A State wishes to provide reservation in promotion for SC and ST employees. Following Nagaraj as described, it must

options.A: obtain the prior approval of the President in each individual case
options.B: collect quantifiable data on backwardness and inadequate representation, and preserve efficiency
options.C: obtain the concurrence of the National Commission for Backward Classes beforehand
options.D: wait for Parliament to fix the percentage of reservation by law

questions.explanation: Nagaraj upheld the amendments subject to quantifiable data and efficiency under Article 335.

questions.question: In a recruitment year, 100 posts are available, of which 50 are reserved. Ten reserved posts from the previous year remain unfilled and are carried forward. Under Article 16(4B), those ten posts

options.A: be filled from the general category, the reservation being exhausted
options.B: lapse and cannot be filled in any later recruitment year
options.C: be added to the 100 vacancies, with the ceiling applied to the combined total
options.D: form a separate class, outside the fifty per cent ceiling applied to the year's 100 vacancies

questions.explanation: Article 16(4B) treats carried-forward vacancies as a separate class outside the ceiling for the year.

questions.question: Rohit belongs to an Other Backward Class, and his family income is below the limit for economically weaker sections. Under Articles 15(6) and 16(6) as described, Rohit

options.A: can claim the EWS reservation only if he falls within the creamy layer
options.B: cannot claim it, since classes covered by Articles 15(4), 15(5) and 16(4) are excluded
options.C: can claim the EWS reservation, since his family income is below the limit
options.D: can claim the EWS reservation in addition to his existing OBC reservation

questions.explanation: The EWS reservation is for economically weaker sections other than classes already covered by Articles 15(4), 15(5) and 16(4).

questions.question: After the One Hundred and Fifth Amendment, a State Government wishing to identify socially and educationally backward classes for its own reservation

options.A: may prepare its own list for State purposes
options.B: must obtain the approval of the National Commission for Backward Classes
options.C: must rely solely on the list prepared by the President
options.D: must wait for Parliament to enact a law identifying such classes

questions.explanation: The 105th Amendment restored the States' power to prepare their own lists, reversing the effect of Jayashree Patil.

passages.title: Political Reservation: the 104th and 106th Amendments and Delimitation
passages.passage: Articles 330 and 332 reserve seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in the House of the People and State Legislative Assemblies. Article 334 limited this reservation to ten years from the commencement of the Constitution, and successive amendments extended it. The Constitution (One Hundred and Fourth Amendment) Act, 2019 extended it until 25 January 2030, but ended the nomination of Anglo-Indian members under Articles 331 and 333. The Constitution (One Hundred and Sixth Amendment) Act, 2023, known as the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, inserted Articles 330A and 332A, reserving one-third of the seats in the House of the People and State Legislative Assemblies for women, and extended the same to the Legislative Assembly of the National Capital Territory of Delhi by amending Article 239AA. One-third of the seats reserved for Scheduled Castes, and of those reserved for Scheduled Tribes, are to be reserved for women of those communities; this forms part of, and is not an addition to, the one-third reservation for women. The reservation does not extend to the Rajya Sabha or the State Legislative Councils. Under the new Article 334A, it will come into effect only after delimitation is undertaken on the basis of the first census taken after the commencement of the Act, and it will cease on the expiry of fifteen years from commencement. Seats reserved for women are to be rotated after each delimitation. Delimitation itself has been constrained. The provisos to Articles 82 and 170, as amended by the Eighty-fourth Amendment (2001), freeze the readjustment of seats among States until the first census after 2026, while the Eighty-seventh Amendment (2003) provided that delimitation within States would use the 2001 Census instead of the 1991 Census. Reservation for women in local bodies, by contrast, has existed since the 73rd and 74th Amendments, under which not less than one-third of seats are reserved.

options.B: the House of the People

options.D: the Legislative Assembly of the National Capital Territory of Delhi

questions.explanation: The passage states that the reservation does not extend to the Rajya Sabha or the State Legislative Councils.

options.A: abolished the reservation of seats for Scheduled Tribes in State Legislative Assemblies altogether
options.B: introduced one-third reservation for women in the House of the People and Assemblies
options.C: ended Anglo-Indian nomination under Articles 331 and 333 and extended SC/ST reservation to 2030
options.D: froze the readjustment of seats among States until the first census after 2026

options.A: immediately on the commencement of the 106th Amendment itself
options.B: after delimitation based on the first census taken after commencement of the Amendment
options.C: from the next general election after commencement, without any delimitation
options.D: after delimitation based on the 2001 Census figures

questions.question: Suppose the House of the People has 540 elected seats, of which 90 are reserved for Scheduled Castes and 45 for Scheduled Tribes. Under the 106th Amendment, the number of seats reserved for women, and the number of those drawn from SC and ST seats, are respectively
questions.explanation: One-third of 540 is 180. Women's seats within SC (one-third of 90 = 30) and ST (one-third of 45 = 15) seats total 45, and form part of the 180.

options.A: on 25 January 2030
options.B: on the expiry of ten years from the commencement of the Amendment
options.C: when the reservation for SC and ST ceases
options.D: on the expiry of fifteen years from the commencement of the Amendment

options.A: The One Hundred and Sixth Amendment
options.B: The Eighty-seventh Amendment
options.C: The Eighty-fourth Amendment
options.D: The One Hundred and Fourth Amendment

questions.explanation: The 84th Amendment amended the provisos to Articles 82 and 170 to freeze the readjustment. The 87th changed the base census for delimitation within States.

passages.title: The 86th and 93rd Amendments: Education and Reservation in Institutions
passages.passage: The Constitution (Eighty-sixth Amendment) Act, 2002 inserted Article 21A, providing that the State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children aged six to fourteen years in such manner as the State may by law determine. It substituted Article 45 so that the State endeavours to provide early childhood care and education to children below six, and added Article 51A(k), making it a fundamental duty of a parent or guardian to provide opportunities for education to a child between six and fourteen. Article 21A took effect on 1 April 2010 when the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 (RTE Act) came into force. The Act requires private unaided schools to reserve twenty-five per cent of entry-level seats for children from weaker and disadvantaged sections. The Court had earlier, in Unni Krishnan v. State of A.P. (1993), held that the right to education up to fourteen flows from Article 21 read with Articles 41 and 45, and that beyond that age it is limited by the State's economic capacity. The Constitution (Ninety-third Amendment) Act, 2005 inserted Article 15(5), enabling special provisions for socially and educationally backward classes, Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in admission to educational institutions, including private unaided institutions, other than minority institutions under Article 30(1). In Ashoka Kumar Thakur v. Union of India (2008), the Court upheld Article 15(5) and the reservation of twenty-seven per cent of seats for OBCs in Central educational institutions, provided the creamy layer was excluded. In Society for Unaided Private Schools of Rajasthan v. Union of India (2012), the Court upheld the twenty-five per cent requirement for non-minority private unaided schools, and in Pramati Educational and Cultural Trust v. Union of India (2014), it held that the RTE Act cannot apply to minority institutions, whether aided or unaided.

questions.question: Article 21A guarantees free and compulsory education to children aged

options.A: five to fourteen years
options.B: six to fourteen years
options.C: six to sixteen years
options.D: three to eighteen years

questions.explanation: Article 21A covers children aged six to fourteen.

questions.question: Article 15(5), enabling special provisions in admission to educational institutions, was inserted by the

options.A: Seventy-seventh Amendment
options.B: One Hundred and Third Amendment
options.C: Eighty-sixth Amendment
options.D: Ninety-third Amendment

questions.explanation: The passage states that the 93rd Amendment (2005) inserted Article 15(5).

questions.question: Under Article 51A(k), the duty to provide opportunities for education to a child between six and fourteen is cast on

options.A: the Gram Sabha
options.B: the parent or guardian
options.C: the school in which the child is enrolled
options.D: the State alone

questions.explanation: Article 51A(k), inserted by the 86th Amendment, makes it a duty of the parent or guardian.

questions.question: A linguistic-minority school, unaided by the State, is asked to reserve twenty-five per cent of its entry-level seats under the RTE Act. Following Pramati as described, this requirement

options.A: applies only for the admission of children belonging to the minority
options.B: applies only if the school begins to receive State aid
options.C: applies, since all unaided schools are covered by the RTE Act
options.D: cannot be applied to it, since the RTE Act does not apply to minority institutions

questions.explanation: Pramati held that the RTE Act cannot apply to minority institutions, aided or unaided.

questions.question: A non-minority private unaided school has 80 seats in its entry-level class. Under the RTE requirement as upheld, the number of seats it must reserve for children from weaker and disadvantaged sections is
questions.explanation: Twenty-five per cent of 80 is 20.

questions.question: A State law reserves seats for OBC candidates in a private unaided engineering college run by a religious minority. Under Article 15(5) as described, this reservation is

options.A: valid, since Article 15(5) extends to all private unaided institutions without exception
options.B: valid, but only if the creamy layer is excluded from the benefit
options.C: outside Article 15(5), which excludes minority institutions under Article 30(1)
options.D: valid, but only if the reservation does not exceed twenty-five per cent of seats

questions.explanation: Article 15(5) covers private unaided institutions but expressly excludes minority institutions under Article 30(1).

passages.title: The 42nd Amendment and the Seventh Schedule: Legislative Relations under Articles 246 to 254
passages.passage: Article 246 distributes legislative power among the Union List (List I), the State List (List II) and the Concurrent List (List III) of the Seventh Schedule. Parliament has exclusive power on List I, the State Legislatures on List II, and both on List III, though a Union law prevails over a State law on a Concurrent subject unless the State law, reserved for the President, receives his assent, in which case it prevails in that State, subject to Parliament's power to legislate again on the same matter (Article 254). Residuary power vests in Parliament (Article 248). The Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976 transferred five subjects from the State List to the Concurrent List: education, forests, protection of wild animals and birds, weights and measures, and administration of justice, including the constitution and organisation of all courts except the Supreme Court and High Courts. It also added population control and family planning to the Concurrent List. Parliament may legislate on a State List subject in four situations: under Article 249, if the Rajya Sabha declares by a resolution supported by two-thirds of the members present and voting that it is necessary in the national interest; during a Proclamation of Emergency under Article 250; with the consent of two or more States under Article 252; and to implement a treaty or international agreement under Article 253. A law made under Article 249 operates for the period of the resolution, which may be up to one year at a time, and ceases six months after the resolution lapses. Courts apply the doctrine of pith and substance: where the true nature of a law falls within the competence of the enacting legislature, it is not invalid merely because it incidentally encroaches on a subject in another List.

questions.question: Which of the following was NOT transferred from the State List to the Concurrent List by the 42nd Amendment?

options.A: Weights and measures
options.B: Police
options.C: Education
options.D: Forests

questions.explanation: The passage lists education, forests, wild animals and birds, weights and measures, and administration of justice. Police remains a State subject.

questions.question: For Parliament to legislate on a State List subject in the national interest under Article 249, the resolution must be passed by

options.A: the Lok Sabha, by two-thirds of the members present and voting
options.B: the Rajya Sabha, by two-thirds of the members present and voting
options.C: the Lok Sabha, by a simple majority
options.D: both Houses, by a simple majority

questions.explanation: Article 249 requires a Rajya Sabha resolution supported by two-thirds of members present and voting.

questions.question: The Rajya Sabha passes an Article 249 resolution to remain in force for one year from 1 January. Laws made under it will cease to have effect

options.A: at the end of one year, on 31 December of the same year
options.B: six months after the resolution lapses, that is, on 1 July of the following year
options.C: on 1 July of the same year
options.D: on the day the Rajya Sabha next meets after the resolution lapses

questions.explanation: The resolution lapses after one year; the laws cease six months later.

questions.question: Parliament and a State Legislature enact conflicting laws on a Concurrent List subject. The State law had been reserved for and received the President's assent. In that State,

options.A: the State law prevails, though Parliament may later legislate again on the same matter
options.B: the State law prevails permanently, and Parliament cannot legislate again on the matter
options.C: both laws are void to the extent of the conflict
options.D: the Union law prevails, notwithstanding the President's assent to the State law

questions.explanation: Under Article 254 as described, assented State law prevails in the State, subject to Parliament's power to legislate again on the same matter.

questions.question: Parliament enacts a law on a State List subject solely to give effect to an international agreement. Under Article 253, the law is

options.A: valid only if two or more States consent to it
options.B: valid only while a Proclamation of Emergency is in force
options.C: valid only if the Rajya Sabha passes an Article 249 resolution
options.D: valid, without a Rajya Sabha resolution or the consent of the States

questions.explanation: Article 253 is an independent source of power to implement treaties and agreements.

questions.question: A State enacts a law whose true nature falls within an entry of the State List but which incidentally touches a matter in the Union List. Under the doctrine of pith and substance, the law is

options.A: valid, since in its true nature it falls within the State's competence
options.B: invalid unless Parliament consents to the encroachment
options.C: valid only if reserved for and assented to by the President
options.D: invalid, since it encroaches on the Union List

questions.explanation: Incidental encroachment does not invalidate a law whose pith and substance is within the enacting legislature's competence.

passages.title: The 99th Amendment, the Collegium and Tribunals
passages.passage: The appointment of judges has produced a sequence of decisions known as the Judges Cases. In S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (1981), the Court held that 'consultation' with the Chief Justice of India in Article 124(2) did not mean concurrence, giving the executive primacy. In Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (1993) (the Second Judges Case), a nine-judge Bench overruled this, holding that the CJI's opinion has primacy, formed through a collegium. In the Third Judges Case (Special Reference No. 1 of 1998, under Article 143), the Court held that the collegium for the Supreme Court consists of the CJI and four senior-most judges. The Constitution (Ninety-ninth Amendment) Act, 2014 inserted Articles 124A, 124B and 124C and set up the National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC) of six members: the CJI as chairperson, two senior-most Supreme Court judges, the Union Law Minister, and two eminent persons nominated by a committee of the Prime Minister, the CJI and the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha. In Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (2015) (the Fourth Judges Case), a Constitution Bench by 4:1 struck down the Amendment and the NJAC Act as violating the basic structure, namely the independence of the judiciary and the separation of powers, and revived the collegium. Justice Chelameswar dissented. Separately, the Forty-second Amendment inserted Articles 323A and 323B for administrative and other tribunals. In L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997), the Court struck down the provisions excluding the jurisdiction of the High Courts under Articles 226 and 227 and of the Supreme Court under Article 32, holding that judicial review is part of the basic structure; decisions of tribunals are subject to scrutiny before a Division Bench of the concerned High Court.

questions.question: The decision which first held that the opinion of the Chief Justice of India has primacy in judicial appointments, formed through a collegium, is

options.A: the Second Judges Case (1993)
options.B: S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (1981)
options.C: the Third Judges Case (1998)
options.D: the Fourth Judges Case (2015)

questions.explanation: S.P. Gupta gave executive primacy; the Second Judges Case overruled it and gave primacy to the CJI.

questions.question: The Ninety-ninth Amendment inserted which Articles to create the NJAC?

options.A: Articles 323A and 323B relating to tribunals
options.B: Articles 143 and 144 relating to advisory jurisdiction
options.C: Articles 217 and 222 relating to High Court judges
options.D: Articles 124A, 124B and 124C

questions.explanation: The passage states that the 99th Amendment inserted Articles 124A, 124B and 124C.

questions.question: Which of the following has NO role in nominating the two eminent persons to the NJAC?

options.A: The Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha
options.B: The Union Law Minister
options.C: The Prime Minister
options.D: The Chief Justice of India

questions.explanation: The nominating committee is the Prime Minister, the CJI and the Leader of the Opposition. The Law Minister is an NJAC member but not on that committee.

questions.question: In the Fourth Judges Case (2015), the Court

options.A: upheld the 99th Amendment and the NJAC Act by 4:1, with one judge dissenting
options.B: struck down the 99th Amendment and the NJAC Act unanimously, with no dissent
options.C: struck down both by 4:1 as violating judicial independence and separation of powers
options.D: struck down the NJAC Act but upheld the 99th Amendment as valid

questions.explanation: A Constitution Bench struck down both by 4:1, with Justice Chelameswar dissenting, and revived the collegium.

questions.question: A litigant is aggrieved by an order of the Central Administrative Tribunal. Following L. Chandra Kumar as described, the proper first course is to approach

options.A: the Supreme Court directly under Article 32
options.B: the President of India
options.C: a Division Bench of the concerned High Court
options.D: a parliamentary committee

questions.explanation: Tribunal decisions are subject to scrutiny before a Division Bench of the concerned High Court.

questions.question: As per the Third Judges Case, the collegium for appointments to the Supreme Court consists of

options.A: the CJI and two senior-most judges
options.B: the CJI and four senior-most judges
options.C: the CJI and all other judges of the Court
options.D: the CJI alone

questions.explanation: The passage states that the collegium for the Supreme Court consists of the CJI and four senior-most judges.

passages.title: Article 368(2): Ratification, the 52nd Amendment and the 97th Amendment
passages.passage: Article 368(2) provides that a Bill to amend the Constitution may be introduced only in either House of Parliament and must be passed in each House by a majority of the total membership and by not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting; the President must then give assent. A proviso adds that where the amendment seeks to change certain federal provisions, it must also be ratified by the legislatures of not less than one-half of the States. These provisions include the election of the President (Articles 54 and 55), the extent of the executive power of the Union and the States, the Supreme Court and the High Courts, the distribution of legislative powers between the Union and the States, any of the Lists in the Seventh Schedule, the representation of States in Parliament, and Article 368 itself. In Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992), the Court held, by a majority of 3:2, that paragraph 7 of the Tenth Schedule, inserted by the Fifty-second Amendment and barring the jurisdiction of courts over disqualification decisions, affected the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court and High Courts and therefore needed ratification, which had not been obtained. Paragraph 7 was held invalid, but being severable, the rest of the Tenth Schedule survived. The Constitution (Ninety-seventh Amendment) Act, 2011 added 'co-operative societies' to Article 19(1)(c), inserted Article 43B, and added a new Part IXB (Articles 243ZH to 243ZT) on co-operative societies. Since 'co-operative societies' is a subject in the State List, the amendment needed ratification, which was not obtained. In Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah (2021), the Supreme Court, by a majority of 2:1, struck down Part IXB insofar as it applied to co-operative societies in the States, but upheld it for multi-State co-operative societies, which fall within Parliament's domain.

questions.question: An amendment affecting the Lists in the Seventh Schedule requires ratification by

options.A: the legislatures of at least half of the States
options.B: the Rajya Sabha acting alone by a special majority
options.C: the legislatures of all the States without exception
options.D: the legislatures of two-thirds of the States

questions.explanation: The proviso to Article 368(2) requires ratification by not less than one-half of the State legislatures.

questions.question: Which of the following amendments would require ratification by State legislatures under the proviso to Article 368(2)?

options.A: One adding a new Fundamental Duty to Article 51A
options.B: One altering a Directive Principle in Part IV
options.C: One altering the Lists in the Seventh Schedule
options.D: One lowering the voting age under Article 326

questions.explanation: The proviso covers changes to the Seventh Schedule Lists; the other subjects are not listed in it.

questions.question: In Kihoto Hollohan, paragraph 7 of the Tenth Schedule was held invalid because

options.A: it ousted court jurisdiction without ratification by the States
options.B: it violated the Fundamental Right to equality under Article 14 of the Constitution
options.C: it was passed by less than two-thirds of the members present and voting
options.D: it imposed an unreasonable restriction on the freedoms under Article 19(1)

questions.explanation: The passage gives the reason: it ousted court jurisdiction, requiring ratification, which was not obtained.

questions.question: A challenge is made to the election of the board of a multi-State co-operative society under Part IXB. After Rajendra N. Shah, Part IXB

options.A: continues to apply to multi-State co-operative societies
options.B: applies only to co-operative societies in the States
options.C: applies only if the States ratify it
options.D: no longer applies to any co-operative society

questions.explanation: The Court struck down Part IXB for State societies but upheld it for multi-State co-operative societies.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the procedure under Article 368(2) as described?

options.A: A Bill may also be introduced in a State Legislature and then sent on to Parliament
options.B: A Bill needs only a simple majority in each House if the President is willing to assent
options.C: If the Rajya Sabha disagrees, the Bill may be passed at a joint sitting of both Houses
options.D: Introduction in either House, then a majority of the total membership and two-thirds of those present and voting

questions.explanation: Article 368(2) requires introduction in Parliament and the special majority in each House, followed by assent. No joint sitting is provided.

questions.question: The Court's treatment of paragraph 7 in Kihoto Hollohan illustrates that

options.A: the whole of the Fifty-second Amendment fell for want of ratification
options.B: ratification is required for every amendment affecting Fundamental Rights
options.C: a defect in one severable provision need not invalidate the whole amendment
options.D: the Tenth Schedule as a whole was held unconstitutional by the Court

questions.explanation: Paragraph 7 was severed and struck down; the rest of the Tenth Schedule survived.

passages.title: Directive Principles, Article 31C and the Preamble: 25th and 42nd Amendments
passages.passage: Part IV of the Constitution contains the Directive Principles, which are not enforceable by courts. In State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951), the Court held that Fundamental Rights prevail over Directive Principles, which must conform to and run as subsidiary to them. The Twenty-fifth Amendment (1971) inserted Article 31C, protecting laws giving effect to the policy in Article 39(b) and (c) from challenge for violation of Articles 14, 19 and 31, and providing that no law containing a declaration that it gives effect to such policy could be questioned in any court on the ground that it does not do so. In Kesavananda Bharati (1973), the second part of that protection was struck down, so that courts may examine whether a law actually gives effect to the policy of Article 39(b) or (c). The Forty-second Amendment (1976) extended Article 31C to laws giving effect to any Directive Principle in Part IV. In Minerva Mills (1980), the Court struck down this extension, holding that harmony and balance between Parts III and IV is part of the basic structure. The 42nd Amendment also inserted Articles 39A (equal justice and free legal aid), 43A (workers' participation in management) and 48A (protection of the environment), and added Part IVA with Article 51A on Fundamental Duties. It inserted the words 'socialist', 'secular' and 'integrity' in the Preamble. Article 39(b) provides that the ownership and control of the material resources of the community should be so distributed as best to subserve the common good. In Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra (2024), a nine-judge Bench held that not every privately owned resource is a 'material resource of the community'; some may qualify depending on factors such as the nature of the resource, its impact on community well-being, scarcity and the consequences of its concentration in private hands.

questions.question: Article 39A, providing for equal justice and free legal aid, was inserted by the

options.A: Eighty-sixth Amendment
options.B: Forty-second Amendment
options.C: Forty-fourth Amendment
options.D: Twenty-fifth Amendment

questions.explanation: The passage lists Article 39A among the Articles inserted by the 42nd Amendment.

questions.question: Which of the following words was NOT inserted into the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment?

options.A: Secular
options.B: Integrity
options.C: Democratic
options.D: Socialist

questions.explanation: The 42nd Amendment inserted 'socialist', 'secular' and 'integrity'. 'Democratic' formed part of the original Preamble.

questions.question: A State law gives effect to Article 48A, and in doing so violates Article 14. The law claims immunity under Article 31C. After Minerva Mills, the claim

options.A: succeeds, since the 42nd Amendment extended Article 31C to all Directive Principles
options.B: succeeds only if the law contains a declaration that it gives effect to Article 48A
options.C: succeeds, since Article 48A was itself inserted by the 42nd Amendment
options.D: fails, since Article 31C protects only laws giving effect to Article 39(b) and (c)

questions.explanation: Minerva Mills struck down the extension of Article 31C beyond Article 39(b) and (c).

questions.question: A statute declares that it gives effect to Article 39(c), but in substance it concentrates wealth and violates Article 14. A court

options.A: may test whether it truly gives effect to Article 39(b) or (c), and deny protection if not
options.B: must uphold the law, since the declaration of its purpose is conclusive on courts
options.C: cannot examine the matter at all, since Article 31C bars all judicial review
options.D: must uphold the law if it was passed by a two-thirds majority in Parliament

questions.explanation: After Kesavananda, courts may examine whether a law actually gives effect to the policy; the declaration is not conclusive.

questions.question: The principle laid down in Champakam Dorairajan is that

options.A: Fundamental Rights prevail over Directive Principles
options.B: Directive Principles prevail over Fundamental Rights
options.C: Directive Principles are enforceable by courts
options.D: Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles are equal in rank

questions.explanation: The Court held that Directive Principles must conform to and run as subsidiary to Fundamental Rights.

questions.question: The 2024 decision in Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra held that

options.A: no privately owned resource can ever fall within the scope of Article 39(b)
options.B: not every privately owned resource qualifies, though some may
options.C: Article 39(b) applies only to resources owned by the Government or its agencies
options.D: all privately owned resources can be redistributed under Article 39(b)

questions.explanation: The Bench rejected both extremes and held that qualification depends on factors such as nature, impact, scarcity and concentration.

passages.title: Elections and the Constitution: the 61st Amendment, Article 324 and Disqualification
passages.passage: The Constitution (Sixty-first Amendment) Act, 1988 reduced the voting age under Article 326 from twenty-one to eighteen years. Article 324 vests the superintendence, direction and control of elections in the Election Commission. The Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) can be removed only in the manner and on the grounds applicable to a Supreme Court judge, while other Election Commissioners can be removed only on the CEC's recommendation (Article 324(5)). Article 329(b) provides that no election to Parliament or a State Legislature shall be called in question except by an election petition. In Mohinder Singh Gill v. Chief Election Commissioner (1978), the Court treated Article 324 as a reservoir of power to act where no law exists. In Anoop Baranwal v. Union of India (2023), a Constitution Bench held that until Parliament makes a law, the CEC and Election Commissioners shall be appointed by the President on the advice of a committee of the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition and the Chief Justice of India. Parliament later enacted the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023, replacing the Chief Justice with a Union Cabinet Minister nominated by the Prime Minister; the Act has been challenged, and its current status should be verified before it is cited. Under Section 8(3) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, a person convicted and sentenced to imprisonment of two years or more is disqualified from the date of conviction and for six years after release. In Lily Thomas v. Union of India (2013), the Court struck down Section 8(4), which allowed sitting legislators to continue pending appeal. Disqualification is not incurred if the appellate court stays the conviction itself, not merely the sentence (Lok Prahari, 2018). In Association for Democratic Reforms v. Union of India (2024), the Court struck down the Electoral Bonds Scheme as violating the voter's right to information under Article 19(1)(a).

questions.question: The 61st Amendment, 1988 reduced the voting age under Article 326 to

options.A: nineteen years
options.B: eighteen years
options.C: twenty years
options.D: twenty-one years

questions.explanation: The passage states that the voting age was reduced from twenty-one to eighteen.

questions.question: A challenge to the validity of an election to the Lok Sabha must, under Article 329(b), be made by

options.A: a civil suit in a District Court
options.B: an election petition
options.C: a writ petition directly under Article 32
options.D: a representation to the Election Commission

questions.explanation: Article 329(b) permits an election to be questioned only by an election petition.

questions.question: Under Article 324(5), an Election Commissioner other than the CEC can be removed

options.A: only in the manner and on the grounds applicable to a Supreme Court judge
options.B: by the Prime Minister on the advice of the Leader of the Opposition
options.C: at the pleasure of the President
options.D: only on the recommendation of the CEC

questions.explanation: Only the CEC enjoys Supreme Court judge-like protection; other Commissioners are removable on the CEC's recommendation.

questions.question: A sitting Member of Parliament is convicted and sentenced to three years' imprisonment. His appeal is pending, and the appellate court stays only the sentence, not the conviction. On the passage, he

options.A: stands disqualified from the date of conviction
options.B: remains qualified until the appeal is decided
options.C: is disqualified only on a decision of the Speaker
options.D: is disqualified only after completing the sentence

questions.explanation: Section 8(3) operates from conviction; Lily Thomas removed the pending-appeal protection, and only a stay of the conviction itself avoids disqualification.

questions.question: The Electoral Bonds Scheme was struck down in 2024 as violating

options.A: the right of adult suffrage under Article 326
options.B: the powers of the Election Commission under Article 324
options.C: the voter's right to information under Article 19(1)(a)
options.D: the donors' right to privacy under Article 21

questions.explanation: The passage states that the Court found a violation of the voter's right to information under Article 19(1)(a).

questions.question: How does the 2023 Act differ from the arrangement laid down in Anoop Baranwal?

options.A: It substitutes a Union Cabinet Minister for the Chief Justice on the selection committee
options.B: It makes the CEC removable at the pleasure of the President of India
options.C: It vests the power of appointment in Parliament acting by resolution
options.D: It removes the Leader of the Opposition from the selection committee altogether

questions.explanation: The passage states that the Chief Justice was replaced with a Cabinet Minister nominated by the Prime Minister.

passages.title: Money Bills and Ordinances: Articles 109, 110 and 123
passages.passage: A Money Bill, defined in Article 110, deals only with matters such as taxes, borrowing and the Consolidated Fund of India. It can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha on the recommendation of the President. After it is passed, it is transmitted to the Rajya Sabha, which must return it within fourteen days with recommendations; the Lok Sabha may accept or reject them, and if the Rajya Sabha does not return the Bill within fourteen days it is deemed to have been passed by both Houses. The Speaker's certificate that a Bill is a Money Bill is made final by Article 110(3), and the provisions for a joint sitting in Article 108 do not apply to Money Bills or Constitution Amendment Bills. In K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (the Aadhaar case, 2018), the majority upheld the Aadhaar Act as a Money Bill, while Justice D.Y. Chandrachud dissented, holding that the route was a fraud on the Constitution because it bypassed the Rajya Sabha. Article 123 empowers the President, at any time except when both Houses are in session, to promulgate an Ordinance when satisfied that immediate action is necessary. An Ordinance has the same force as an Act of Parliament, must be laid before both Houses, and ceases to operate at the expiration of six weeks from the reassembly of Parliament, or earlier if both Houses pass resolutions disapproving it. An Ordinance cannot amend the Constitution. In D.C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987), the Court held that the repeated re-promulgation of Ordinances without placing them before the Legislature is a fraud on the Constitution, a view affirmed by a seven-judge Bench in Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar (2017), which also held that rights and liabilities that arose during the life of a lapsed Ordinance do not automatically vanish. Article 213 confers a similar power on Governors.

questions.question: The Rajya Sabha must return a Money Bill to the Lok Sabha within

options.A: 14 days
options.B: 30 days
options.C: 6 weeks
options.D: 6 months

questions.explanation: The passage states that the Rajya Sabha must return a Money Bill within fourteen days, failing which it is deemed passed.

questions.question: The joint sitting under Article 108 cannot be used for

options.A: any Bill rejected by the Rajya Sabha
options.B: Bills introduced in the Rajya Sabha
options.C: Money Bills and Constitution Amendment Bills
options.D: Ordinary Bills passed by the Lok Sabha

questions.explanation: The passage states that Article 108 does not apply to Money Bills or Constitution Amendment Bills.

questions.question: In the Aadhaar case, Justice Chandrachud's dissent held that

options.A: Money Bills may validly be introduced in the Rajya Sabha as well
options.B: the Aadhaar Act violated only the freedom under Article 19
options.C: the Speaker's certificate under Article 110(3) is conclusive and unreviewable by courts
options.D: the Money Bill route bypassed the Rajya Sabha and was a fraud on the Constitution

questions.explanation: The passage records his view that the Money Bill route bypassed the Rajya Sabha and was a fraud on the Constitution.

questions.question: An Ordinance is promulgated while Parliament is in recess, and Parliament reassembles on 1 March. Assuming no disapproving resolutions, the Ordinance ceases to operate on

options.A: 31 March
options.B: 1 April
options.C: 12 April
options.D: 1 May

questions.explanation: It ceases six weeks (42 days) after reassembly: 1 March plus 42 days is 12 April.

questions.question: A State Government has the Governor promulgate the same Ordinance four times in succession without placing it before the Legislature. Under D.C. Wadhwa, this practice is

options.A: valid for six months only
options.B: valid if the Council of Ministers approves each re-promulgation
options.C: a fraud on the Constitution and invalid
options.D: valid, so long as the Governor is satisfied each time

questions.explanation: Wadhwa held that repeated re-promulgation without placing the Ordinance before the Legislature is a fraud on the Constitution.

questions.question: Only one House of Parliament is in session. On Article 123 as described, the President

options.A: may promulgate an Ordinance, as the bar applies only when both Houses sit
options.B: may not promulgate an Ordinance, since one House is in session
options.C: may promulgate an Ordinance only on a request made by the Speaker
options.D: may promulgate an Ordinance only after first summoning the other House

questions.explanation: Article 123 bars an Ordinance only when both Houses are in session.

passages.title: Hohfeld's Jural Relations and Legal Personality
passages.passage: Wesley Hohfeld analysed legal relations into eight fundamental conceptions arranged as jural correlatives and jural opposites. The correlatives are: right and duty; privilege (liberty) and no-right; power and liability; immunity and disability. The jural opposites are: right and no-right; privilege and duty; power and disability; immunity and liability. A 'right' in the strict sense is a claim that another person owes a duty; a privilege is freedom from any duty to the contrary, so that others have no claim against the holder; a power is the ability to change legal relations, as an offeree changes the position of an offeror by accepting; and an immunity is freedom from having one's legal relations changed by another's act. Salmond defined a legal right as an interest recognised and protected by a rule of law. Legal personality extends beyond natural persons. In Salomon v. Salomon & Co. (1897), the House of Lords held that a duly incorporated company is a separate legal person distinct from its members, though courts may lift the veil where the company is a sham or is used for fraud. In Yogendra Nath Naskar v. CIT (1969), the Supreme Court held that a Hindu idol is a juristic person capable of holding property, and in Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee v. Som Nath Dass (2000), the Guru Granth Sahib was held to be a juristic person. In Mohd. Salim v. State of Uttarakhand (2017), the Uttarakhand High Court declared the Ganga and Yamuna to be legal persons, though the Supreme Court stayed that order. In Animal Welfare Board of India v. A. Nagaraja (2014), the Supreme Court held that the right to life under Article 21 includes the right of animals to dignity and humane treatment.

questions.question: In Hohfeld's scheme, the jural correlative of a right is

options.A: a liability
options.B: a no-right
options.C: a privilege
options.D: a duty

questions.explanation: Right and duty are correlatives. No-right is the jural opposite of a right.

questions.question: In Yogendra Nath Naskar v. CIT, the Supreme Court held that a Hindu idol is

options.A: a mere chattel incapable of owning property
options.B: a trust but not a juristic person
options.C: a natural person with full capacity to contract
options.D: a juristic person capable of holding property

questions.explanation: The passage states that the idol was held to be a juristic person capable of holding property.

questions.question: An offeree who accepts an offer alters the legal position of the offeror. In Hohfeldian terms, the offeree exercises a ____ and the offeror is under a ____.

options.A: power; liability
options.B: right; duty
options.C: immunity; disability
options.D: privilege; no-right

questions.explanation: Power is the ability to change legal relations; its correlative is liability.

questions.question: A judge enjoys immunity from civil suit for judicial acts. In Hohfeld's scheme, the correlative position of an aggrieved litigant is

options.A: a disability
options.B: a duty
options.C: a liability
options.D: a no-right

questions.explanation: Immunity and disability are correlatives; liability is the opposite of immunity.

questions.question: A may walk across a public footpath, and no one has a claim that he refrain from doing so. A's position is a

options.A: right, and others have a duty
options.B: privilege, and others have a no-right
options.C: power, and others have a liability
options.D: immunity, and others have a disability

questions.explanation: A privilege is freedom from any duty to the contrary, and its correlative is no-right.

questions.question: X is the sole shareholder of a company that defaults on a loan. The creditor sues X personally, with no allegation of fraud or sham. Under Salomon as described, the claim

options.A: succeeds, since the veil can be lifted in any case of default on a debt
options.B: fails only if X was not a director of the company at the time
options.C: succeeds, since a sole shareholder is in law identical to the company
options.D: fails, since the company is a separate person and X is not personally liable

questions.explanation: The veil may be lifted only for sham or fraud; mere default does not engage the shareholder.

passages.title: General Principles of Criminal Liability under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita
passages.passage: Criminal liability generally requires a prohibited act (actus reus) and a guilty mind (mens rea), expressed in the maxim actus non facit reum nisi mens sit rea. The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS), in force from 1 July 2024, replaced the Indian Penal Code, 1860. Section 3(5) BNS (IPC section 34) provides that when a criminal act is done by several persons in furtherance of the common intention of all, each is liable as if he alone had done it; it requires a prior meeting of minds, though that may occur on the spot, and it can apply to even two persons. Section 190 BNS (IPC section 149) provides that if an offence is committed by any member of an unlawful assembly in prosecution of its common object, or such as the members knew to be likely to be committed in prosecution of that object, every member is guilty of it. An unlawful assembly under section 189 requires five or more persons. Abetment under section 45 BNS includes instigation, conspiracy and intentional aid. Under section 61 BNS, an agreement to commit an offence is itself a criminal conspiracy; but for an agreement to do an illegal act that is not an offence, or a legal act by illegal means, some act besides the agreement is required. Section 103(1) BNS punishes murder with death or imprisonment for life and fine, and section 103(2) provides that when a group of five or more persons acting in concert commits murder on the ground of race, caste or community, sex, place of birth, language, personal belief or any other similar ground, each member of the group shall be punished with death or imprisonment for life and fine.

questions.question: The maxim actus non facit reum nisi mens sit rea emphasises that criminal liability generally requires

options.A: a prohibited act alone, irrespective of intention
options.B: strict liability for every offence
options.C: a guilty mind together with a prohibited act
options.D: a guilty mind alone, irrespective of any act

questions.explanation: The maxim states that an act does not make a person guilty unless the mind is also guilty.

questions.question: The minimum number of persons required for an unlawful assembly under section 189 BNS is

options.A: ten
options.B: two
options.C: three
options.D: five

questions.explanation: The passage states that an unlawful assembly requires five or more persons.

questions.question: Five persons form an assembly with the common object of beating X. In prosecution of that object, one of them stabs and kills X, a result the others knew to be likely. Under section 190 BNS, the other four are

options.A: guilty only of attempt to cause hurt to X
options.B: guilty only if there was a prior meeting of minds under section 3(5) of the BNS
options.C: not guilty, since only the stabber committed the act itself
options.D: guilty of the offence, as members of the assembly who knew it was likely

questions.explanation: Section 190 fastens liability on every member for offences committed in prosecution of the common object, or such as the members knew to be likely.

questions.question: A principal difference between common intention (section 3(5)) and common object (section 190) is that

options.A: common intention requires five or more persons, whereas common object can be shared by two
options.B: common object needs an assembly of five or more, common intention can be shared by two
