options.C: common object requires a prior meeting of minds, whereas common intention does not
options.D: common intention creates no liability at all, while common object does

questions.explanation: Section 190 depends on an unlawful assembly of five or more; section 3(5) can apply to two persons and requires a prior meeting of minds.

questions.question: Four persons acting in concert kill a man on the ground of his caste. On the passage, the offence is

options.A: murder under section 103(2), punishable with death or imprisonment for life
options.B: murder under section 103(1), as the group provision needs five or more persons
options.C: culpable homicide not amounting to murder, the group being small
options.D: no offence at all, since the group is smaller than five persons

questions.explanation: Section 103(2) needs a group of five or more; with four, ordinary murder under section 103(1) applies.

questions.question: A and B agree to commit theft but take no further step. Under section 61 BNS as described, they are

options.A: not guilty, since no act beyond the agreement was done
options.B: guilty of criminal conspiracy, the agreement itself being enough
options.C: guilty only of attempt to commit theft
options.D: guilty only of abetment by instigation of the other

questions.explanation: An agreement to commit an offence is complete conspiracy without an overt act; the overt act requirement applies to other agreements.

passages.title: Formation of Contract, Consideration, Minors and Frustration
passages.passage: Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a proposal becomes a promise when accepted. The display of goods with prices in a shop is an invitation to treat, not an offer, and a quotation of price is not an offer (Harvey v. Facey). A general offer to the world can be accepted by performance, as in Carlill v. Carbolic Smoke Ball Co. (1893). Acceptance by post is complete as against the proposer when the letter is put into the course of transmission, and a proposal may be revoked at any time before the communication of its acceptance is complete as against the proposer (sections 4 and 5). Under section 2(d), consideration is what the promisor desires the promisee or any other person to do or abstain from, and it may be past, present or future. Consideration may move from a third party, but only a party can enforce the contract; a stranger to the contract cannot sue (privity), subject to exceptions such as a trust or a family arrangement. Section 25(2) makes a promise to compensate a person who has already voluntarily done something for the promisor enforceable without fresh consideration. A minor's agreement is void ab initio (Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose, 1903) and cannot be ratified on attaining majority. Under section 56, a contract to do an act that after the contract becomes impossible or unlawful becomes void; in Satyabrata Ghose v. Mugneeram Bangur (1954), the Court held that 'impossible' extends to the destruction of the foundation of the contract. In Alopi Parshad v. Union of India (1960), a mere rise in cost or unforeseen difficulty was held not to frustrate a contract.

questions.question: The display of goods with prices in a shop window is

options.A: an offer
options.B: an acceptance
options.C: an invitation to treat
options.D: a concluded contract

questions.explanation: The passage states that display of goods with prices is an invitation to treat.

questions.question: Under Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose, an agreement with a minor is

options.A: valid but unenforceable against the minor
options.B: valid if ratified on attaining majority
options.C: void ab initio
options.D: voidable at the option of the minor

questions.explanation: The passage states that a minor's agreement is void ab initio and cannot be ratified.

questions.question: A offers to sell a plot to B by letter. B posts a letter of acceptance on Monday. A's telegram revoking the offer, sent after B posted the letter, reaches B on Tuesday. Under sections 4 and 5, the contract is

options.A: not concluded, since A revoked before the acceptance reached him
options.B: concluded, since acceptance was complete against A when posted
options.C: concluded only when A actually reads the letter of acceptance
options.D: voidable at A's option, the offer having been revoked in time

questions.explanation: Acceptance is complete as against the proposer when posted; revocation must precede that moment.

questions.question: A contracts with B that B will pay Rs 1,00,000 to C, a friend of A. B fails to pay. C sues B on the contract. On the passage, C's suit

options.A: succeeds, since consideration may move from a third party
options.B: succeeds, since C is the intended beneficiary of the promise
options.C: fails only if B had no knowledge of C's interest
options.D: fails, since a stranger to the contract cannot sue absent a trust

questions.explanation: Under privity, only a party can enforce the contract; consideration moving from a third party does not make the third party a party.

questions.question: S agrees to supply 1,000 tonnes of cement to B. A war raises transport costs by forty per cent, but delivery remains possible. Following Alopi Parshad as described, the contract

options.A: becomes voidable at S's option
options.B: stands discharged on grounds of commercial impracticability
options.C: becomes void under section 56
options.D: is not frustrated, and S must perform

questions.explanation: A mere rise in cost or unforeseen difficulty does not frustrate a contract.

questions.question: A voluntarily and without request saves B's house from a fire. A month later B promises to pay A Rs 10,000 for the help. On section 25(2) as described, the promise is

options.A: enforceable only if B had asked for the help beforehand
options.B: enforceable, as it compensates one who voluntarily did something for the promisor
options.C: unenforceable, since past consideration is no consideration in India
options.D: enforceable only if the promise is made in a registered document

questions.explanation: Section 25(2) makes such a promise enforceable without fresh consideration.

passages.title: Vicarious Liability and State Liability in Tort
passages.passage: Vicarious liability makes an employer liable for torts committed by an employee in the course of employment. An act is within the course of employment if it is authorised, or is an unauthorised mode of doing an authorised act (Limpus v. London General Omnibus Co.). Article 300(1) provides that the Government of India or a State may sue or be sued, and that its liability shall be the same as it would have been had the Constitution not been enacted. This refers to the position of the East India Company, whose liability was examined in P. & O. Steam Navigation Co. v. Secretary of State for India (1861), which distinguished acts done in exercise of sovereign powers from other acts. In State of Rajasthan v. Vidyawati (1962), the State was held vicariously liable for the negligent driving of a government jeep by its driver, since the driving was not an exercise of sovereign power. In Kasturilal Ralia Ram Jain v. State of U.P. (1965), the State was held not liable for the loss of gold seized by the police, because the seizure was an exercise of sovereign power delegated by statute. In N. Nagendra Rao & Co. v. State of A.P. (1994), the Court confined sovereign immunity to acts strictly referable to inalienable sovereign functions and found the State liable for negligent care of seized goods. Independently, constitutional courts award compensation as a public law remedy for violation of Fundamental Rights, as in Rudul Sah (1983) and Nilabati Behera v. State of Orissa (1993), a custodial death case, where sovereign immunity was held to be no defence; such compensation does not bar a civil suit in tort.

questions.question: The provision which allows the Union and the States to sue and be sued is

options.A: Article 32
options.B: Article 299
options.C: Article 226
options.D: Article 300(1)

questions.explanation: The passage states that Article 300(1) provides that the Government of India or a State may sue or be sued.

questions.question: In State of Rajasthan v. Vidyawati, the State was held

options.A: vicariously liable for its driver's negligent driving of a government jeep
options.B: immune, since the jeep was Government property and not a private vehicle
options.C: liable only if the driver was a permanent employee of the State
options.D: immune, since the driver was performing a sovereign function at the time

questions.explanation: The passage states that driving was not an exercise of sovereign power, so the State was liable.

questions.question: A patient is injured by the negligence of a surgeon in a Government hospital. On the passage, the State is

options.A: immune, since the hospital is run by the State itself
options.B: liable only if Parliament has enacted a law imposing such liability
options.C: immune, since the surgeon acts under a statute governing hospitals
options.D: vicariously liable, as medical treatment is not a sovereign function

questions.explanation: Following Vidyawati and Nagendra Rao, liability is excluded only for acts strictly referable to inalienable sovereign functions.

questions.question: In a writ petition arising from a custodial death, the High Court awards compensation, and the State pleads sovereign immunity. Under Nilabati Behera as described, the plea

options.A: succeeds, since a High Court cannot award damages in writ jurisdiction
options.B: succeeds, since custody is an exercise of sovereign power under Kasturilal
options.C: fails, but the compensation then bars any later civil suit in tort
options.D: fails, since sovereign immunity is no defence to public law compensation

questions.explanation: Nilabati Behera held that immunity is no defence, and the passage states that such compensation does not bar a civil suit.

questions.question: A bus conductor, trying to eject a passenger who refuses to pay the fare, pushes him off a moving bus and injures him. The employer is

options.A: liable, since the act was an unauthorised mode of doing an authorised act
options.B: liable only if the employer was present
options.C: not liable, since the conductor was not authorised to push passengers
options.D: liable only if the employer ordered the act

questions.explanation: Under the Limpus test, an unauthorised mode of doing an authorised act is within the course of employment.

questions.question: The distinction between sovereign and non-sovereign functions under Article 300(1) traces its origin to

options.A: Kasturilal Ralia Ram Jain v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1965)
options.B: State of Rajasthan v. Vidyawati (1962)
options.C: P. & O. Steam Navigation Co. v. Secretary of State (1861)
options.D: Nilabati Behera v. State of Orissa (1993)

questions.explanation: The passage states that the East India Company's liability was examined in P. & O. Steam Navigation, which drew the distinction.

passages.title: Electronic Evidence: Section 65B, Section 63 BSA and Arjun Panditrao Khotkar
passages.passage: Electronic records are admissible in evidence, but their admissibility depends on compliance with statutory conditions. Under section 65B of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, an electronic record produced by a computer is admissible as a document only if the prescribed conditions are met and a certificate accompanies it. The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA), in force from 1 July 2024, replaced the Evidence Act, and section 63 BSA re-enacts the rule, with a certificate in the Schedule in two parts: Part A signed by the party or the person in charge of the device, and Part B by an expert; the certificate must also state the hash value of the record. In Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer (2014), the Supreme Court held that electronic records produced as secondary evidence are inadmissible unless accompanied by the section 65B certificate. In Shafhi Mohammad v. State of H.P. (2018), the Court relaxed this where the party does not hold the device. A three-judge Bench in Arjun Panditrao Khotkar v. Kailash Kushanrao Gorantyal (2020) overruled Shafhi Mohammad, holding that the certificate is a condition precedent for secondary electronic evidence. The certificate is not needed when the original device is itself produced in court and proved by its owner, since that is primary evidence. Where the device or the certificate is held by a third party who refuses to give it, the party may apply to the court to direct its production, since the law does not require the impossible. The BSA also provides that electronic or digital records have the same legal effect, validity and enforceability as paper records.

questions.question: The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 replaced the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 with effect from

options.A: 1 January 2024
options.B: 15 August 2023
options.C: 1 April 2024
options.D: 1 July 2024

questions.explanation: The passage states that the BSA has been in force from 1 July 2024.

questions.question: The Supreme Court held that a section 65B certificate is necessary for secondary electronic evidence in

options.A: Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan
options.B: Mohinder Singh Gill v. Chief Election Commissioner
options.C: Shafhi Mohammad v. State of H.P.
options.D: Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer

questions.explanation: Anvar P.V. (2014) held that such records are inadmissible without the certificate. Shafhi Mohammad relaxed the rule.

questions.question: Which decision was overruled by Arjun Panditrao Khotkar?

options.A: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India
options.B: Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer
options.C: Shafhi Mohammad v. State of H.P.
options.D: K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India

questions.explanation: The three-judge Bench overruled Shafhi Mohammad and reaffirmed the certificate requirement.

questions.question: A witness brings her own mobile phone to court, produces it, and proves it as the original device holding the recording. On the passage, a section 65B certificate is

options.A: required, since all electronic evidence needs a certificate in every case
options.B: not required, as production of the original device is primary evidence
options.C: required, but only Part B signed by an expert
options.D: required, but only if the opposing party objects to the recording

questions.explanation: The passage states that no certificate is needed when the original device is produced and proved by its owner.

questions.question: Under the Schedule to the BSA, Part B of the certificate is signed by

options.A: an expert
options.B: the presiding Judge
options.C: the Registrar of the High Court
options.D: a Magistrate

questions.explanation: Part A is signed by the party or person in charge of the device; Part B by an expert.

questions.question: A litigant relies on call records held by a telecom company that refuses to issue a certificate. As described under Arjun Panditrao, the litigant

options.A: can never rely on the call records without the certificate
options.B: may rely on the records as secondary evidence without any certificate at all
options.C: may apply to the court to direct production, since the law does not require the impossible
options.D: must first obtain the telecom company's consent before approaching the court

questions.explanation: The passage states that where a third party holds the certificate and refuses, the court can be asked to direct production.

passages.title: Leases, Mortgages and Easements
passages.passage: Under section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a lease is a transfer of a right to enjoy immovable property for a certain time, express or implied, or in perpetuity, in consideration of a price paid or promised. Under section 107, a lease of immovable property from year to year, for any term exceeding one year, or reserving a yearly rent, can be made only by a registered instrument. A lease is distinguished from a licence, which under section 52 of the Indian Easements Act, 1882 merely gives a right to do something on another's property without creating an interest in it; the test is whether exclusive possession was granted (Associated Hotels of India v. R.N. Kapoor, 1959). Under section 106, a lease of immovable property for agricultural or manufacturing purposes is terminable on six months' notice, and a lease for any other purpose on fifteen days' notice, the lease being treated as year to year or month to month respectively. A mortgage under section 58 is the transfer of an interest in specific immovable property to secure the payment of money, and takes six forms: simple, by conditional sale, usufructuary, English, by deposit of title deeds (equitable) and anomalous. An equitable mortgage can be created in specified towns by delivery of title deeds with intent to create security and needs no registered instrument. Section 60 gives the mortgagor the right to redeem on payment, and a stipulation that postpones or defeats that right is a 'clog on redemption' and void, in keeping with the maxim 'once a mortgage, always a mortgage'. An easement under the Indian Easements Act is a right of the owner of the dominant heritage, for its beneficial enjoyment, to do or prevent something on the servient heritage; it can be acquired by peaceable and open enjoyment as of right, without interruption, for twenty years, and thirty years against the Government.

questions.question: A lease of immovable property for a term exceeding one year can be made only by

options.A: an oral agreement
options.B: an unregistered written agreement
options.C: mere delivery of possession
options.D: a registered instrument

questions.explanation: Section 107 requires a registered instrument for such a lease.

questions.question: A mortgage created by the deposit of title deeds is called

options.A: an anomalous mortgage
options.B: a usufructuary mortgage
options.C: an English mortgage
options.D: an equitable mortgage

questions.explanation: The passage identifies the mortgage by deposit of title deeds as the equitable mortgage.

questions.question: An owner grants B exclusive possession of a room for a monthly payment for eleven months. In deciding whether this is a lease or a licence, the decisive test is

options.A: the length of the period
options.B: whether exclusive possession was granted
options.C: the label the parties give the document
options.D: whether the payment is made monthly

questions.explanation: Following Associated Hotels, the test is whether exclusive possession was granted.

questions.question: A mortgage deed provides that the mortgagor may not redeem the property until fifty years have passed, although the loan is repayable in five. This stipulation is

options.A: valid, since the parties are free to agree on any term
options.B: valid if the deed is registered
options.C: void as a clog on the right of redemption
options.D: valid only in a usufructuary mortgage

questions.explanation: A stipulation postponing the right to redeem is a clog on redemption and void.

questions.question: For seventeen years, B has openly and peaceably used a footpath across A's private land as of right, without interruption. B's claim to an easement by prescription

options.A: has not matured, since thirty years are required against a private owner
options.B: has not matured, since twenty years of enjoyment are required
options.C: has matured, since ten years are enough
options.D: has matured, since a footpath needs no minimum period

questions.explanation: Twenty years are needed against a private owner; thirty only against the Government.

questions.question: A manufacturer holds a factory shed on lease with no stated term. The notice required for the lessor to terminate the lease is

options.A: fifteen days
options.B: one month
options.C: six months
options.D: three months

questions.explanation: A lease for manufacturing purposes is treated as year to year and terminable on six months' notice; fifteen days applies to other purposes.

passages.title: Coparcenary, Intestate Succession and Gifts under Hindu and Muslim Law
passages.passage: The Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 substituted section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, so that in a joint Hindu family governed by the Mitakshara law, the daughter of a coparcener becomes by birth a coparcener in her own right, with the same rights and liabilities as a son. In Prakash v. Phulavati (2016), the Court required that the father should have been alive on 9 September 2005, the date of commencement. A three-judge Bench in Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020) overruled that view, holding that the right is by birth and does not depend on whether the father was alive on that date. The Court also held that an oral partition is not accepted unless supported by public documents, and that a partition after 20 December 2004 must be by a registered deed or a decree of court. Section 15 deals with the property of a Hindu female dying intestate: it goes first to sons, daughters (including children of predeceased children) and the husband; then to the heirs of the husband; then to the mother and father; then to the heirs of the father; and lastly to the heirs of the mother. But under section 15(2), property she inherited from her father or mother goes, in the absence of children, to the heirs of her father, and property inherited from her husband or father-in-law goes, in the absence of children, to the heirs of her husband. Under Muslim law, a person may by will dispose of only one-third of the estate without the consent of the heirs, and a gift (hiba) requires a declaration by the donor, acceptance by the donee and delivery of possession.

questions.question: Under section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act as substituted in 2005, the daughter of a coparcener

options.A: becomes a coparcener by birth, with the same rights as a son
options.B: becomes a coparcener only on the death of her father
options.C: has the right to maintenance but not to a coparcenary share
options.D: becomes a coparcener only on her marriage

questions.explanation: The passage states that the daughter becomes a coparcener by birth in her own right.

questions.question: Under Muslim law, a person can by will dispose of, without the consent of the heirs, at most

options.A: one-half of the estate
options.B: one-third of the estate
options.C: two-thirds of the estate
options.D: the entire estate

questions.explanation: The passage states that the limit is one-third of the estate without the heirs' consent.

questions.question: A Hindu coparcener died in 2001. His daughter claims coparcenary rights in 2015. Under Vineeta Sharma as described, she

options.A: is a coparcener by birth, even though her father died before 9 September 2005
options.B: is a coparcener only if she was unmarried in 2001
options.C: is entitled only to maintenance
options.D: is not a coparcener, since her father was not alive on 9 September 2005

questions.explanation: Vineeta Sharma overruled the requirement that the father be alive on 9 September 2005.

questions.question: A Hindu woman dies intestate, leaving neither husband nor children. The property she had inherited from her father goes to

options.A: the heirs of her husband
options.B: the heirs of her mother
options.C: the heirs of her father
options.D: the State

questions.explanation: Under section 15(2), property inherited from her father goes, in the absence of children, to the heirs of her father.

questions.question: In 2012, brothers claim that the ancestral property was partitioned orally in 1998 and rely on this to defeat their sister's claim to a coparcenary share. There is no public document supporting the alleged partition. Under Vineeta Sharma as described, the plea of oral partition is

options.A: accepted if two witnesses testify to it
options.B: accepted, since partition before 20 December 2004 needs no proof
options.C: accepted, since an oral partition made before 2005 is always valid
options.D: not accepted without support of public documents, so her claim is not defeated

questions.explanation: An oral partition is not accepted unless supported by public documents.

questions.question: A Muslim donor declares a gift of a house to his nephew, who accepts it, but the donor continues in possession and never delivers it. The gift is

options.A: valid if the gift deed is registered
options.B: invalid for want of delivery of possession
options.C: valid, since declaration and acceptance suffice
options.D: valid if two witnesses attest it

questions.explanation: A hiba requires declaration, acceptance and delivery of possession.

passages.title: Company Law: Ultra Vires, Indoor Management, Foss v. Harbottle and Oppression
passages.passage: A company incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013 acts through its Memorandum and Articles, which are public documents; a person dealing with the company is deemed to have constructive notice of them. An act beyond the objects clause of the Memorandum is ultra vires and void (Ashbury Railway Carriage Co. v. Riche). The doctrine of indoor management in Royal British Bank v. Turquand protects an outsider dealing in good faith, who may assume that internal procedures have been complied with. The doctrine does not protect a person who has actual or constructive knowledge of the irregularity, a person put on inquiry by suspicious circumstances, or a transaction founded on forgery. Under Foss v. Harbottle, the court will not interfere in the internal management of a company at the instance of a minority, since the majority rules; exceptions include acts that are ultra vires or illegal, fraud on the minority by those in control, and infringement of members' personal rights. Sections 241 and 242 allow members to apply to the National Company Law Tribunal for relief against oppression and mismanagement. Under section 244, in a company having share capital, the application may be made by not less than one hundred members or one-tenth of the total number of members, whichever is less, or by members holding at least one-tenth of the issued share capital, subject to payment of calls; the Tribunal may waive these requirements. Section 149 requires that at least one-third of the total number of directors of a listed public company be independent directors, any fraction being rounded off as one. Fraud under section 447 is punishable with imprisonment which shall not be less than six months but may extend to ten years, and fine.

questions.question: The doctrine of indoor management protects

options.A: directors from personal liability for company debts
options.B: the company from claims by outsiders
options.C: minority shareholders from oppression
options.D: outsiders who deal in good faith with a company

questions.explanation: The doctrine allows an outsider dealing in good faith to assume that internal procedures were complied with.

questions.question: An act of a company which is beyond the objects clause of its Memorandum is

options.A: valid, since the directors authorised it
options.B: ultra vires and void
options.C: voidable at the option of the company
options.D: valid if ratified by an ordinary resolution

questions.explanation: The passage states that such an act is ultra vires and void.

questions.question: A company secretary forges the signatures of two directors on a share certificate and sells the shares to P, who acts in good faith. Under the passage, the company

options.A: is bound, since P had no notice of the forgery and acted in good faith
options.B: is not bound, since indoor management does not protect forgery
options.C: is bound, since the secretary has ostensible authority to sell shares
options.D: is bound, since the Articles are public documents available to P

questions.explanation: Indoor management does not extend to forgery.

questions.question: Directors who control the majority sell a valuable asset of the company to themselves at a throwaway price. A minority shareholder may

options.A: not sue, since the rule of majority control is absolute and admits no exception
options.B: only seek the winding up of the company, and nothing else
options.C: sue, as fraud on the minority by those in control is an exception to Foss v. Harbottle
options.D: only complain to the Registrar of Companies, who alone can act in the matter

questions.explanation: Fraud on the minority by those in control is a recognised exception to Foss v. Harbottle.

questions.question: A company with share capital has 600 members. Ignoring the issued-capital route and any waiver by the Tribunal, the minimum number of members who can apply under section 244 for relief against oppression is
questions.explanation: The requirement is one hundred members or one-tenth of the members, whichever is less. One-tenth of 600 is 60, which is less than 100.

questions.question: A listed public company has a board of ten directors. The minimum number of independent directors required under section 149 is
questions.explanation: One-third of ten is 3.33, and the fraction is rounded off as one, giving four.

passages.title: Sources of International Law, the Law of the Sea and India's Constitutional Engagement
passages.passage: Article 38 of the Statute of the International Court of Justice lists the sources of international law: treaties, international custom as evidence of a general practice accepted as law, and general principles of law recognised by civilised nations, with judicial decisions and the teachings of publicists as subsidiary means. Custom requires both consistent State practice and opinio juris, the belief that the practice is legally obligatory (North Sea Continental Shelf Cases, 1969). Peremptory norms (jus cogens) permit no derogation. In the Lotus case (1927), the Permanent Court held that restrictions on the independence of States cannot be presumed. In the Nottebohm case (1955), the ICJ held that a State may exercise diplomatic protection of a person only where there is a genuine link of nationality. Under UNCLOS, 1982, a coastal State's sovereignty extends to a territorial sea of up to twelve nautical miles, subject to the right of innocent passage; the contiguous zone extends to twenty-four nautical miles; and in the Exclusive Economic Zone, extending to two hundred nautical miles, the coastal State has sovereign rights over natural resources, though other States enjoy freedom of navigation. In the Enrica Lexie arbitration (2020), an Annex VII tribunal held that the Italian marines enjoyed immunity for acts committed while on duty, so that India could not exercise jurisdiction, but that India was entitled to compensation. In Kulbhushan Jadhav (India v. Pakistan) (2019), the ICJ held Pakistan in breach of Article 36 of the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations and directed effective review and reconsideration of his conviction and sentence, without ordering release. Article 51(c) of the Indian Constitution directs the State to foster respect for international law and treaty obligations, and in Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997), the Supreme Court used international conventions to fill a legislative vacuum, reading them into Articles 14, 15, 19 and 21 where consistent with them.

questions.question: Under UNCLOS as described, a coastal State's territorial sea extends up to

options.A: 6 nautical miles
options.B: 12 nautical miles
options.C: 24 nautical miles
options.D: 200 nautical miles

questions.explanation: The passage states that the territorial sea extends up to twelve nautical miles.

questions.question: The provision of the Indian Constitution which directs the State to foster respect for international law and treaty obligations is

options.A: Article 51(c)
options.B: Article 246
options.C: Article 21
options.D: Article 253

questions.explanation: The passage states that Article 51(c) contains this direction.

questions.question: A group of States consistently follows a practice of dipping flags to a particular type of vessel, but only out of courtesy and not from any sense of legal obligation. The practice

options.A: becomes binding as a treaty between those States
options.B: becomes custom, since the practice is consistent
options.C: becomes a peremptory norm binding on all States
options.D: does not become custom, since opinio juris is lacking

questions.explanation: Custom requires both consistent State practice and opinio juris.

questions.question: State Z grants citizenship to a businessman against a fee, though he has never lived there. He is harmed in State Y, and Z espouses his claim. Under Nottebohm as described, Y may

options.A: object only if Y is a party to the UNCLOS regime
options.B: object that there is no genuine link of nationality with Z
options.C: object only if the businessman is otherwise a stateless person
options.D: not object, since the grant of nationality is for Z alone to decide

questions.explanation: Nottebohm requires a genuine link for the exercise of diplomatic protection.

questions.question: A foreign trawler is found fishing without a licence 150 nautical miles off India's coast. On UNCLOS as described, India

options.A: has sovereign rights over the living resources of its EEZ and may regulate the fishing
options.B: has no rights, since this area forms part of the high seas
options.C: has full territorial sovereignty over that area as over its land territory
options.D: may act only if the trawler claims a right of innocent passage through the area

questions.explanation: 150 nautical miles lies within the 200-nautical-mile EEZ, where the coastal State has sovereign rights over natural resources.

questions.question: In Kulbhushan Jadhav (India v. Pakistan), the ICJ

options.A: found no breach of the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations
options.B: ordered his release and repatriation to India without delay
options.C: found a breach of Article 36 and ordered review, not release
options.D: held his conviction void ab initio and set it aside altogether

questions.explanation: The passage states the breach finding and the direction for review and reconsideration, without release.

passages.title: Delegated Legislation and Natural Justice
passages.passage: Delegated legislation consists of rules, regulations and bye-laws made by an executive authority under power conferred by a statute. In Re Delhi Laws Act (1951), the Supreme Court held that the legislature cannot delegate its essential legislative functions, though it may delegate ancillary power. In Hamdard Dawakhana v. Union of India (1960), a provision conferring unguided power on the Central Government to specify diseases was struck down for lack of legislative policy. In Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985), the Court held that delegated legislation may be challenged on the grounds available against plenary legislation, and also on the ground that it conflicts with the parent Act or the Constitution or is manifestly arbitrary. Whether a requirement to lay rules before the legislature is mandatory or directory depends on the statute, and courts have generally treated it as directory where laying is only for information. Natural justice has two limbs: nemo judex in causa sua, the rule against bias, and audi alteram partem, the right to a fair hearing. In Ridge v. Baldwin (1964), the House of Lords insisted on a hearing before the dismissal of a police chief. In A.K. Kraipak v. Union of India (1969), the Supreme Court held that the distinction between administrative and quasi-judicial functions is blurred, and that the presence on a selection board of a member who was himself a candidate vitiated the selection. In Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), the Court held that natural justice is implicit in Article 14, and that where an authority acts urgently, a post-decisional hearing may satisfy the requirement. In S.N. Mukherjee v. Union of India (1990), the Court held that administrative authorities exercising quasi-judicial power must record reasons.

questions.question: In Re Delhi Laws Act, the Supreme Court held that the legislature

options.A: may delegate only to the judiciary, and to no other authority
options.B: cannot delegate essential functions, but may delegate ancillary power
options.C: may delegate any legislative function without limit to the executive
options.D: may delegate only with the prior assent of the President

questions.explanation: The passage states that essential legislative functions cannot be delegated.

questions.question: The maxim audi alteram partem refers to

options.A: the right to a fair hearing
options.B: the duty to give reasons
options.C: the doctrine of legitimate expectation
options.D: the rule against bias

questions.explanation: Audi alteram partem is the right to be heard; nemo judex is the rule against bias.

questions.question: In a selection process, a member of the selection board is himself a candidate and sits on the board when his own name is considered. On Kraipak as described, the selection is

options.A: valid, since the member is a public officer
options.B: valid, since the function is purely administrative
options.C: vitiated by bias
options.D: valid unless the member voted for himself

questions.explanation: Kraipak held that such presence vitiated the selection and that the administrative/quasi-judicial distinction is blurred.

questions.question: A rule made under an Act conflicts with a provision of the parent Act. Under Indian Express Newspapers as described, the rule is

options.A: valid if laid before the legislature
options.B: valid unless it is shown to be unreasonable
options.C: valid, since the delegate has wide rule-making power
options.D: liable to be struck down as conflicting with the parent Act

questions.explanation: Delegated legislation may be challenged for conflict with the parent Act or the Constitution.

questions.question: A statute requires rules to be laid before Parliament for information only, with no power to modify them. Rules are notified but not laid. Courts have generally treated the requirement as

options.A: directory, so that non-laying does not by itself invalidate them
options.B: satisfied only on the assent of the President to the rules
options.C: fatal only if Parliament later disapproves the rules by resolution
options.D: mandatory, so that the rules are void for non-laying

questions.explanation: The passage states that courts have generally treated laying as directory where it is only for information.

questions.question: A passport is impounded urgently in the public interest, and a hearing is offered only after the impounding. On Maneka Gandhi as described, this procedure

options.A: needs no hearing at all, since a passport is a mere privilege
options.B: may satisfy natural justice, since urgency allows a post-decisional hearing
options.C: is valid only during a Proclamation of Emergency
options.D: is invalid, since a prior hearing is always required

questions.explanation: The passage states that in urgent cases a post-decisional hearing may satisfy the requirement.

passages.title: Copyright and Trade Marks: Originality, Moral Rights and Registrability
passages.passage: Under the Copyright Act, 1957, copyright subsists in original literary, dramatic, musical and artistic works, and generally lasts for the life of the author plus sixty years. Copyright protects expression, not ideas (R.G. Anand v. Deluxe Films, 1978). In Eastern Book Company v. D.B. Modak (2008), the Supreme Court rejected the 'sweat of the brow' standard in favour of a 'modicum of creativity', holding that headnotes and copy-edited judgments showing sufficient creativity were protected, but not the judgments themselves. Section 57 confers on the author special rights, independent of the ownership of copyright, to claim authorship and to restrain distortion, mutilation or modification prejudicial to honour or reputation; in Amar Nath Sehgal v. Union of India (2005), the destruction of a mural was held to violate these moral rights. Section 52 lists acts that are not infringement, including fair dealing for private use, research, criticism, review and the reporting of current events. Under the Trade Marks Act, 1999, a mark is registered for ten years, renewable. Section 9 lists absolute grounds for refusal: marks devoid of distinctive character, descriptive of the goods, or customary in trade, unless the mark has acquired distinctiveness through use. Section 11 lists relative grounds, such as likelihood of confusion with an earlier mark. Passing off protects unregistered marks against misrepresentation causing damage. In Cadila Health Care Ltd. v. Cadila Pharmaceuticals Ltd. (2001), the Court held that, where medicinal products are concerned, a stricter standard applies in assessing deceptive similarity, because confusion may endanger health.

questions.question: Under the Copyright Act, 1957, copyright in a literary work generally lasts for

options.A: the life of the author plus 25 years
options.B: the life of the author plus 50 years
options.C: the life of the author plus 60 years
options.D: 100 years from publication

questions.explanation: The passage states that copyright generally lasts for the life of the author plus sixty years.

questions.question: Following R.G. Anand v. Deluxe Films, copyright protects

options.A: the idea, but not its expression
options.B: both the idea and its expression equally
options.C: the expression of an idea, not the idea itself
options.D: neither ideas nor their expression

questions.explanation: Copyright protects expression, not ideas.

questions.question: A compiles an alphabetical list of names from a public telephone directory, with no selection or creative arrangement. Under the 'modicum of creativity' test of Eastern Book Company, A's compilation

options.A: enjoys copyright because of the effort invested in compiling it
options.B: enjoys copyright for a period of ten years only
options.C: enjoys copyright by virtue of the moral rights in section 57
options.D: is unlikely to enjoy copyright, as mere labour is not enough

questions.explanation: Eastern Book rejected the sweat of the brow standard in favour of a modicum of creativity.

questions.question: A sculptor sells a statue and assigns the copyright in it. The buyer later mutilates the statue, to the prejudice of the sculptor's reputation. Under section 57, the sculptor

options.A: has no remedy, since he has assigned the copyright to the buyer
options.B: has a remedy only while he still owns the statue
options.C: has a remedy only under the Trade Marks Act
options.D: may still restrain it, as moral rights exist independently of copyright

questions.explanation: Section 57 rights exist independently of ownership of copyright.

questions.question: A applies to register the word 'SWEET' for confectionery, with no evidence of acquired distinctiveness. The Registrar is likely to refuse registration under

options.A: section 52, as an act that is not infringement of copyright
options.B: section 9, being descriptive and devoid of distinctive character
options.C: section 57, as a violation of the author's moral rights
options.D: section 11, for likelihood of confusion with an earlier mark

questions.explanation: Section 9 bars marks that are descriptive or devoid of distinctive character unless distinctiveness is acquired.

questions.question: Two cough syrups are sold under similar brand names. In assessing deceptive similarity, following Cadila Health Care, the Court would apply

options.A: a stricter standard, since confusion between medicines may endanger health
options.B: the same standard as applies to confectionery
options.C: a lower standard, since pharmacists are careful
options.D: no standard at all, since a registered mark cannot be challenged

questions.explanation: The Court held that a stricter standard applies to medicinal products.
